Issued at 156 AM CDT Thu Oct 15 2026

Today... Our two upper level waves continue to approach this 
morning and the combined synoptic support from these waves will 
be a part of the widespread rain chances today. At the surface,
a low will travel across the Great Plains to the southern Great
Lakes. This low track will have one the main deformation axes 
over us and provide for a large area of stratiform rainfall. 
With the low track this axis will generally setup from south 
central Minnesota into west central Wisconsin. Rain will be 
possible farther northwest of this axis, but the amounts will be
lower. Overall this feels much more like the kind of systems we
see during the winter, which as we are in October now is not 
surprising, as this is deformation driven precipitation and we 
expect some lighter wrap around precipitation afterwards as 
well. Looking toward the model guidance there is much better 
agreement with both the RRFS and HRRR having a similar footprint
of the QPF. Looking towards the ensembles there remain some 
difference between the HREF and REFS with the REFS slightly 
farther east. HREF PMM has the southeast Twin Cities metro as 
the edge of highest QPF, but the REFS has this farther east into
Wisconsin. Overall rainfall is likely along a Fairmont to 
Mankato to Twin Cities axis with chances dropping off to the 
northwest. Southeast of this axis is where the highest QPF with 
totals of 0.5-1" are expected based on these PMM from the CAM 
ensembles. Forecast soundings show a setup for stratiform rain 
with a well saturated sounding and little instability to support
thunderstorms. This is supported with SPC outlooks that do not 
have us in general thunder.

Tomorrow and Saturday... As the surface low departs some
additional light rain could occur with some wrap around in the
morning. In general, Friday will be driven by CAA associated 
with a high moving in to our west. The impact from this high will
be cold air and gusty winds. The peak of the CAA should come to
an end by the evening and that should help bring the gusts 
down. However this keeps the CAA strong during the daytime 
heating keeping highs down in the lower 50s. Then under the high
pressure light winds and clear skies will allow for ample 
radiational cooling Friday night into Saturday morning. This
creates a favorable setup for frost and freeze. Based on our 
current forecast and guidance a freeze looks like it could occur
everywhere outside of the urban core of the Twin Cities. Even 
in the urban core a frost still looks likely. Clear skies look 
to continue into the day which should allow for warming, 
especially as the the flow aloft starts to shift towards WAA 
later in the day.

Next Week... This period is driven by persistent ridging with 
an uncertain end point. The ridging will persist through 
mid week with some guidance suggesting we could see our next 
wave late next week, but spread remains. What this means for 
the weather is warm, much above normal temperatures, return 
along with few if any chances for rain. So after our coldest air
of the season so far Friday into Saturday morning we look to go
right back into the warmth. Normal highs next week fall into the
mid 50s and our forecast currently has mid to upper 60s. So ten
or more degree above normal which could drive our current,
already high, departure even higher for the month. We will need
to keep on eye on records for October, as another week of 10+
degree above normal temperatures could put us in reach of a 
record warm month. A lot can change in a short time in fall 
though, but it will take a big shift in the last week of the 
month to make a dent in how warm it has been.
